title: The Anatomy of a Persuasive Argument
text:
An argumentative essay does more than describe a topic; it takes a clear position and defends it with evidence. The writer usually begins with a thesis statement, which summarises the claim the essay intends to prove. Each body paragraph then develops one supporting reason, backed by facts, expert opinions, or logical reasoning. Strong essays also acknowledge the opposing view, since a concession can make the writer appear fair and well-informed.

Anticipating counterarguments is therefore a sign of intellectual maturity rather than weakness. A writer who ignores objections risks being dismissed by readers who already hold a different view. Effective essays address these objections directly and then explain, through a rebuttal, why the original claim still stands. The final paragraph should reinforce the thesis without simply repeating it, leaving the reader with a clear sense of what should now be believed or done.

questions.text: According to the passage, what does a thesis statement summarise?
options: The sources listed at the end of the essay
The claim the essay intends to prove
The opinions of the opposing side
The conclusion of the final paragraph

questions.text: What does the passage say may happen when a writer ignores objections?
options: The writer must rewrite the introduction

questions.text: What can be inferred about the purpose of addressing counterarguments?
options: It shows the writer has considered other perspectives and can respond to them
It proves the opposing view is wrong
It allows the writer to avoid providing evidence

questions.text: What can be inferred about the role of the final paragraph?
options: It should introduce new evidence unrelated to the thesis
It should reinforce the thesis in a new way rather than copy it
It should summarise only the opposing argument
It should be the shortest part of the essay

vocabulary.definition: the central claim a text sets out to prove
an admission that a point made by the opposing side has some merit
a reply that argues against an objection and shows it is wrong

paragraph_translations: Um ensaio argumentativo faz mais do que descrever um tema; ele assume uma posição clara e a defende com evidências. O autor geralmente começa com uma tese, que resume a afirmação que o ensaio pretende provar. Cada parágrafo de desenvolvimento apresenta então um motivo de apoio, sustentado por fatos, opiniões de especialistas ou raciocínio lógico. Textos fortes também reconhecem o ponto de vista contrário, pois uma concessão pode fazer o autor parecer justo e bem informado.

Antecipar contra-argumentos é, portanto, um sinal de maturidade intelectual e não de fraqueza. Um autor que ignora objeções corre o risco de ser descartado por leitores que já defendem outra visão. Ensaios eficazes tratam essas objeções diretamente e depois explicam, por meio de uma refutação, por que a afirmação original continua de pé. O parágrafo final deve reforçar a tese sem simplesmente repeti-la, deixando o leitor com uma noção clara do que deve agora ser acreditado ou feito.
